questions.q: Camphor dissolved in nitrogen gas is classified as which type of solution?
questions.hint: The solvent (nitrogen) is a gas, so it is a gaseous solution; the solute camphor is a solid.
questions.whyTier: Classifying solutions by the physical state of solute and solvent is taken directly from NCERT Table 1.1.
opts: A. Liquid solution with a solid solute
B. Solid solution with a gaseous solute
C. Gaseous solution with a solid solute
D. Gaseous solution with a liquid solute

questions.q: The component of a solution that determines the physical state in which the solution exists is called the ________.
questions.answer: solvent
questions.whyTier: It is the examinable NCERT definition of solvent.

questions.q: An amalgam of mercury with sodium is a liquid solution because mercury is a liquid.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: It is a solid solution: the liquid (mercury) is the solute and the solid (sodium) is the solvent.
questions.whyTier: It targets a common misconception about which component decides the type of solution.

questions.q: Match each solution in Column A with its solute–solvent type in Column B.
questions.whyTier: All four examples come straight from NCERT Table 1.1.

questions.q: Identify the odd one out on the basis of the type of solution.
questions.answer: Hydrogen in palladium
questions.hint: It is a solid solution (gas in solid); the other three are liquid solutions.
questions.whyTier: It is a sorting/classification task, which is a Tier 2 reasoning format.

questions.q: What is meant by a binary solution?
questions.answer: A binary solution is a solution consisting of only two components, one solute and one solvent.
questions.whyTier: It is a direct NCERT definition used in one-mark questions.

questions.q: Distinguish between a solute and a solvent, giving one example of each from a common solution.
questions.answer: The solvent is the component present in the largest quantity and it determines the physical state of the solution; the solute is the component(s) present in smaller quantity other than the solvent. For example, in a glucose solution in water, water is the solvent and glucose is the solute.
questions.whyTier: Definitions of solute and solvent are examinable NCERT content.

questions.q: Case Study: Solutions in everyday materials
questions.passage: Gold jewellery is rarely made of pure gold; copper is dissolved in it to make it harder, giving a uniform solid. Dentists once filled cavities with amalgams in which mercury is mixed with other metals. The air we breathe is itself a mixture of oxygen and nitrogen with uniform composition throughout. Hydrogen gas can also be absorbed by palladium metal, forming a homogeneous solid.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Name the type of solution formed when copper is dissolved in gold.
subqs.answer: A solid solution (solid in solid).

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: Air contains about 21 parts oxygen per 100 parts by volume. Which component of air acts as the solvent and why?
subqs.answer: Nitrogen, since it is present in the largest proportion (about 78%) in air.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why is air considered a solution and not a heterogeneous mixture?
subqs.answer: Because its composition and properties are uniform throughout, which is the defining feature of a homogeneous mixture (solution).

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: If hydrogen absorbed in palladium were later released as a separate gas phase, would the system still be a solution? Explain.
subqs.answer: No. Once hydrogen separates into its own gas phase, the system is no longer uniform (it has two phases), so it is no longer a single homogeneous solution.

questions.q: Which of the following concentration terms depends on temperature?
questions.hint: Molarity uses the volume of solution, and volume changes with temperature.
questions.whyTier: Temperature dependence of concentration terms is stated directly in NCERT and is frequently asked.

questions.q: Molality is the number of moles of solute dissolved per ________ of the solvent.
questions.answer: kilogram
questions.whyTier: It completes an NCERT definition.

questions.q: A concentration of 1 ppm by mass means 1 g of solute is present in 10⁶ g of solution.
questions.answer: True
questions.hint: Parts per million = (parts of component / total parts of solution) × 10⁶.
questions.whyTier: Tests the NCERT definition of ppm.

questions.q: Match each concentration term with its definition.
questions.whyTier: All formulas appear directly in NCERT (equations 1.1–1.9).

pairs.R: (Mass of component / total mass of solution) × 100
Moles of component / total moles of all components
Moles of solute / volume of solution in litre
Moles of solute / mass of solvent in kg

questions.q: Identify the odd one out.
questions.answer: Molarity
questions.hint: Molarity is temperature dependent; the other three depend only on masses and are independent of temperature.
questions.whyTier: It requires classifying terms by a finer property, a Tier 2 reasoning task.

questions.q: Why is molality preferred to molarity when a solution is studied over a range of temperatures?
questions.answer: Molality is based on mass of solvent, which does not change with temperature, whereas molarity is based on volume, which changes with temperature.
questions.whyTier: Directly based on the NCERT statement on merits and demerits of concentration terms.

questions.q: Give two differences between molarity and molality of a solution.
questions.answer: 1. Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution, while molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. 2. Molarity depends on temperature because volume changes with temperature, while molality is independent of temperature because mass does not change.
questions.whyTier: Comparison of molarity and molality is a standard CBSE 2-mark question.

questions.q: Show that in a binary solution of A and B the sum of the mole fractions is unity, and express x_A in terms of the moles n_A and n_B.
questions.answer: Step 1: By definition, x_A = n_A/(n_A + n_B) and x_B = n_B/(n_A + n_B).\nStep 2: Adding, x_A + x_B = (n_A + n_B)/(n_A + n_B).\nStep 3: Therefore x_A + x_B = 1, so x_A = n_A/(n_A + n_B) = 1 − x_B. The result generalises to x₁ + x₂ + … + xᵢ = 1 for i components.
questions.whyTier: The relation Σxᵢ = 1 is an NCERT equation (1.7).

questions.q: Calculate the mole fraction of methanol (CH₃OH) and of water in a solution containing 16 g of methanol and 54 g of water.
questions.answer:
Given: mass of CH₃OH = 16 g (M = 32 g mol⁻¹); mass of water = 54 g (M = 18 g mol⁻¹).
Formula: x_A = n_A/(n_A + n_B).
Substitution: n(CH₃OH) = 16 g / 32 g mol⁻¹ = 0.50 mol; n(H₂O) = 54 g / 18 g mol⁻¹ = 3.00 mol.
x(CH₃OH) = 0.50/(0.50 + 3.00) = 0.143; x(H₂O) = 1 − 0.143 = 0.857.
Answer: x(methanol) = 0.143, x(water) = 0.857.
questions.whyTier: It uses the chapter formula with values not taken from NCERT examples.

questions.q: 10.6 g of sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) is dissolved in water to make 250 mL of solution of density 1.10 g mL⁻¹. Calculate (a) the molarity, (b) the molality and (c) the mass percentage of Na₂CO₃ in the solution.
questions.answer:
Given: w₂ = 10.6 g, M(Na₂CO₃) = 106 g mol⁻¹, V = 250 mL = 0.250 L, density = 1.10 g mL⁻¹.
Moles of Na₂CO₃ = 10.6 g / 106 g mol⁻¹ = 0.100 mol.
(a) Molarity = moles of solute / volume in L = 0.100 mol / 0.250 L = 0.400 mol L⁻¹ (0.400 M).
(b) Mass of solution = 250 mL × 1.10 g mL⁻¹ = 275 g; mass of water = 275 g − 10.6 g = 264.4 g = 0.2644 kg.
Molality = 0.100 mol / 0.2644 kg = 0.378 mol kg⁻¹.
(c) Mass % = (10.6 g / 275 g) × 100 = 3.85%.
questions.whyTier: It is a standard NCERT-style multi-step numerical on interconversion of concentration terms.
keyPoints: Mass of solvent from density = 264.4 g

questions.q: Sketch, on the same axes, how the molarity and the molality of an aqueous solution change as its temperature is raised from 20 °C to 60 °C. Justify the shapes.
questions.answer: Molality is a horizontal straight line (constant) because it depends only on masses. Molarity is a line that slopes slightly downward with rising temperature because the volume of the solution increases on heating while the moles of solute stay the same.
questions.whyTier: It applies the temperature dependence to a graph, an extended reasoning task.

questions.q: Case Study: Concentrations in medicine and water supply
questions.passage: Normal saline used in hospital drips is labelled 0.9% (w/V) sodium chloride. Municipal water boards add fluoride to drinking water at about 1 ppm because this level prevents tooth decay, while higher levels mottle teeth. Chemists in the laboratory prefer molality when they heat or cool solutions during experiments. Each field picks the concentration unit that suits its needs.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: What does a label of 0.9% (w/V) NaCl mean?
subqs.answer: 0.9 g of NaCl is dissolved in every 100 mL of the solution.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: Calculate the mass of NaCl present in a 500 mL bottle of normal saline.
subqs.answer: 0.9 g per 100 mL × 500 mL = 4.5 g of NaCl.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why is fluoride in water expressed in ppm rather than in percentage?
subqs.answer: Fluoride is present in trace quantities, so ppm gives a convenient number (1 ppm) instead of a very small percentage (0.0001%).

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: If some water evaporated from an open saline bottle, how would its molarity change? Explain.
subqs.answer: Molarity would increase, because the same moles of NaCl would now be present in a smaller volume of solution.

questions.q: The solubility of a substance in a solvent does NOT depend on:
questions.hint: Solubility is a fixed maximum for given solute, solvent, temperature and pressure; excess undissolved solid does not change it.
questions.whyTier: The factors affecting solubility are stated directly in NCERT section 1.3.
opts: A. The nature of the solute
B. The nature of the solvent
D. The amount of undissolved solute left at the bottom

questions.q: Solubility of a substance is its maximum amount that can be dissolved in a specified amount of solvent at a specified ________.
questions.answer: temperature
questions.whyTier: It completes the NCERT definition of solubility.

questions.q: For every solute–solvent pair, solubility is independent of pressure.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: Pressure has little effect on solids in liquids but greatly affects the solubility of gases in liquids.
questions.whyTier: It targets a misconception that NCERT explicitly corrects.

questions.q: Match each term with its correct description.
questions.whyTier: All four definitions appear directly in the NCERT text.

pairs.R: Maximum amount of solute dissolved in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature
No more solute can dissolve at the same temperature and pressure
More solute can still be dissolved at the same temperature
Rate of dissolution equals rate of crystallisation

questions.q: Identify the factor that does NOT change the solubility of a given solute.
questions.answer: Volume of solvent taken in the beaker
questions.hint: Solubility is expressed per fixed amount of solvent, so using more solvent dissolves more solute but does not change the solubility itself.
questions.whyTier: It tests a finer feature of the definition of solubility.
opts: Volume of solvent taken in the beaker

questions.q: Define a saturated solution.
questions.answer: A saturated solution is one in which no more solute can be dissolved at the same temperature and pressure; it is in dynamic equilibrium with undissolved solute.
questions.whyTier: It is a key NCERT definition.

questions.q: Why is it necessary to state both temperature and pressure when quoting the solubility of a substance?
questions.answer: Solubility of a solid changes with temperature, and the solubility of a gas changes strongly with both temperature and pressure. A solubility value is therefore meaningful only for the stated temperature and pressure.
questions.whyTier: It requires extended reasoning about the definition rather than recall.

questions.q: The solubility of potassium nitrate at 313 K is 64 g per 100 g of water. Calculate (a) the maximum mass of KNO₃ that can dissolve in 250 g of water at this temperature and (b) the mass percentage of KNO₃ in the saturated solution.
questions.answer:
Given: solubility = 64 g KNO₃ per 100 g water at 313 K; mass of water = 250 g.
Formula: maximum mass = solubility × (mass of water/100 g); mass % = (mass of solute/mass of solution) × 100.
(a) Maximum mass = 64 g × 250 g/100 g = 160 g.
(b) Saturated solution has 64 g KNO₃ in 164 g solution: mass % = (64/164) × 100 = 39.0%.
Answer: 160 g; 39.0%.
questions.whyTier: It combines solubility with mass percentage using values not in NCERT.

questions.q: Case Study: Growing copper sulphate crystals
questions.passage: A student adds copper sulphate to 100 g of hot water, stirring until some solid remains undissolved at the bottom. The clear solution is poured into a clean dish and left to cool overnight. By morning, blue crystals have formed on a thread suspended in the dish. The remaining liquid still looks blue.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: What is the solution called when solid stays undissolved despite stirring?
subqs.answer: A saturated solution.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: If the solubility falls from 40 g to 20 g per 100 g water on cooling, what mass of crystals can form from the 100 g of water?
subqs.answer: 40 g − 20 g = 20 g of crystals.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why do crystals form as the solution cools?
subqs.answer: Solubility decreases on cooling, so the solution holds more solute than it can at the lower temperature and the excess crystallises out.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: Is the liquid left in the dish in the morning saturated or unsaturated? Justify.
subqs.answer: It is saturated at the lower temperature, because it is in equilibrium with the crystals that formed.

questions.q: Which of the following dissolves most readily in benzene?
questions.hint: Like dissolves like: non-polar naphthalene dissolves in non-polar benzene.
questions.whyTier: It applies the NCERT 'like dissolves like' examples.

questions.q: The process in which dissolved solute particles collide with the solid solute and separate out of solution is called ________.
questions.answer: crystallisation
questions.whyTier: It is a key NCERT term.

questions.q: If the dissolution of a solid in a nearly saturated solution is exothermic (Δ_sol H < 0), its solubility increases with rise in temperature.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: By Le Chatelier's principle, solubility decreases with temperature for an exothermic dissolution.
questions.whyTier: It tests a classic misconception about temperature and solubility.

questions.q: Match each condition with its effect on the solubility of a solid in a liquid.
questions.whyTier: Each statement appears directly in NCERT section 1.3.1.

pairs.R: Solubility increases with rise in temperature
Solubility decreases with rise in temperature

questions.q: Which of these is the odd one out with respect to solubility in water?
questions.answer: Anthracene
questions.hint: Anthracene is non-polar and does not dissolve in water; the others are polar/ionic and water-soluble.
questions.whyTier: It is a classification task requiring reasoning.

questions.q: State the principle 'like dissolves like'.
questions.answer: A solute dissolves in a solvent if the intermolecular interactions in the two are similar, so polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents and non-polar solutes in non-polar solvents.
questions.whyTier: It is a direct NCERT principle.

questions.q: Why does pressure have no significant effect on the solubility of a solid in a liquid?
questions.answer: Solids and liquids are highly incompressible, so changing the pressure barely changes their volumes or the equilibrium between dissolved and undissolved solute. Hence solubility practically remains unaffected.
questions.whyTier: The reason is stated directly in NCERT.

questions.q: Using Le Chatelier's principle, explain how a change in temperature affects the solubility of a solid in a nearly saturated solution.
questions.answer: 1. Dissolution reaches a dynamic equilibrium: Solute + Solvent ⇌ Solution.\n2. If dissolution is endothermic (Δ_sol H > 0), raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium forward to absorb heat, so solubility increases.\n3. If dissolution is exothermic (Δ_sol H < 0), raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium backward, so solubility decreases. These trends are observed experimentally.
questions.whyTier: Applying Le Chatelier's principle to solubility is explained in NCERT and is commonly examined.

questions.q: A student plots solubility (g per 100 g water) against temperature for salt X (Δ_sol H > 0) and salt Y (Δ_sol H < 0). Describe the shape of each curve.
questions.answer: The curve for X rises with temperature (solubility increases) because its dissolution is endothermic. The curve for Y falls with temperature (solubility decreases) because its dissolution is exothermic.
questions.whyTier: It requires interpreting a graph not drawn in NCERT.

questions.q: At 333 K, 100 g of water dissolves at most 110 g of a salt; at 293 K it dissolves only 32 g. If 105 g of the saturated solution at 333 K is cooled to 293 K, what mass of salt crystallises out?
questions.answer:
Given: solubility 110 g/100 g water at 333 K; 32 g/100 g water at 293 K; 105 g saturated solution.
Step 1: At 333 K, 110 g salt is in 210 g solution, so 105 g solution has 55 g salt and 50 g water.
Step 2: At 293 K, 50 g water can hold 32 × 50/100 = 16 g salt.
Step 3: Mass crystallising = 55 g − 16 g = 39 g.
Answer: 39 g of the salt crystallises.
questions.whyTier: It is a student-constructed problem needing an extra step beyond NCERT.

questions.q: Case Study: Cleaning grease and salt stains
questions.passage: A mechanic finds that grease on his hands does not wash off with water but comes off easily with kerosene. Salt spilled on the workbench, however, dissolves quickly in a bucket of water but not in kerosene. Warm water dissolves the sugar in his tea faster and in larger amounts than cold water. He wonders why different liquids clean different stains.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: State the principle that explains why grease dissolves in kerosene.
subqs.answer: Like dissolves like: non-polar grease dissolves in non-polar kerosene.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: Is the dissolution of sugar in water more likely endothermic or exothermic? Give a reason from the passage.
subqs.answer: Endothermic, because more sugar dissolves in warm water, i.e. solubility increases with temperature.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why does salt not dissolve in kerosene?
subqs.answer: Salt is ionic/polar while kerosene is non-polar, so their intermolecular interactions are not similar.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: What would happen if the mechanic pressed the salt and water together under high pressure? Explain.
subqs.answer: Almost nothing would change, because pressure has no significant effect on the solubility of solids in liquids, both being nearly incompressible.

questions.q: The Henry's law constant K_H of a gas in water increases as the temperature rises. This indicates that the solubility of the gas:
questions.hint: Higher K_H at a given pressure means lower mole fraction of the dissolved gas, i.e. lower solubility.
questions.whyTier: The K_H–solubility relation is stated directly in NCERT with Table 1.2.
opts: C. Does not depend on temperature
D. First increases and then decreases

questions.q: According to Henry's law, the partial pressure of a gas in the vapour phase is proportional to its ________ in the solution.
questions.answer: mole fraction
questions.whyTier: It completes the NCERT statement of Henry's law.

questions.q: At a given pressure, the higher the value of K_H, the higher is the solubility of the gas in the liquid.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: x = p/K_H, so a higher K_H gives a lower mole fraction, i.e. lower solubility.
questions.whyTier: It targets a frequent misconception about K_H.

questions.q: Match each phenomenon with its explanation based on Henry's law.
questions.whyTier: All applications are discussed in NCERT.

pairs.R: Nitrogen bubbles form in blood as pressure decreases on ascent
Low partial pressure of oxygen lowers oxygen in blood

pairs.L: Soda bottles sealed under high pressure

pairs.R: Reduces the toxic effects of dissolved nitrogen

questions.q: Based on Henry's law constants at 298 K, which gas is the odd one out?
questions.answer: Formaldehyde
questions.hint: Its K_H (1.83 × 10⁻⁵ kbar) is extremely small, so it is far more soluble in water than the others.
questions.whyTier: It requires comparing data from Table 1.2, a reasoning task.

questions.q: Why are aquatic species more comfortable in cold water than in warm water?
questions.answer: The solubility of oxygen in water is higher at lower temperature, so cold water holds more dissolved oxygen.
questions.whyTier: It is an 'explain why' application directly from NCERT.

questions.q: Explain why the solubility of a gas in a liquid decreases with increase in temperature.
questions.answer: 1. When a gas dissolves, its molecules move into the liquid phase; the process is similar to condensation, so heat is evolved (dissolution is exothermic).\n2. Dissolution is a dynamic equilibrium, so it follows Le Chatelier's principle.\n3. Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic (reverse) direction, releasing dissolved gas, so solubility decreases.
questions.whyTier: The explanation is given in NCERT and is a common 3-mark question.

questions.q: The Henry's law constant for oxygen in water at 303 K is 46.82 kbar. Calculate the mole fraction of oxygen dissolved in water when the partial pressure of oxygen above it is 0.21 bar.
questions.answer:
Given: K_H = 46.82 kbar = 46820 bar; p(O₂) = 0.21 bar.
Formula: p = K_H x, so x = p/K_H.
Substitution: x(O₂) = 0.21 bar / 46820 bar.
Answer: x(O₂) = 4.49 × 10⁻⁶.
questions.whyTier: It uses the Henry's law formula with a value from Table 1.2 but a new pressure.

questions.q: The Henry's law constant for CO₂ in water at 298 K is 1.67 kbar. Calculate the mass of CO₂ dissolved in 1 litre (1000 g) of water when the partial pressure of CO₂ over it is 2.0 bar.
questions.answer:
Given: K_H = 1.67 kbar = 1670 bar; p(CO₂) = 2.0 bar; 1000 g water = 1000/18 = 55.5 mol.
Step 1 (Henry's law): x(CO₂) = p/K_H = 2.0 bar / 1670 bar = 1.20 × 10⁻³.
Step 2: x = n/(n + 55.5) ≈ n/55.5, since n << 55.5.
Step 3: n(CO₂) = 1.20 × 10⁻³ × 55.5 mol = 6.65 × 10⁻² mol.
Step 4: Mass of CO₂ = 6.65 × 10⁻² mol × 44 g mol⁻¹ = 2.93 g.
Answer: about 2.93 g of CO₂ dissolves in 1 L of water.
questions.whyTier: It is a standard NCERT-style Henry's law numerical with new values.

questions.q: A graph of the partial pressure of HCl gas against its mole fraction in cyclohexane at 293 K is a straight line through the origin. What does the slope of this line represent, and what law does the graph verify?
questions.answer: The straight line through the origin verifies Henry's law (p = K_H x). Its slope equals the Henry's law constant K_H for HCl in cyclohexane at 293 K.
questions.whyTier: It interprets NCERT Fig. 1.2 directly.

questions.q: Case Study: Diving safely
questions.passage: A recreational diver descends to 30 m, where the surrounding pressure is about four times atmospheric pressure. Breathing compressed air at this depth makes more nitrogen dissolve in the blood. If the diver rises too quickly, bubbles of nitrogen form in the blood vessels, causing a painful condition. Professional divers therefore breathe air diluted with helium.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Name the law that governs how much nitrogen dissolves in blood.
subqs.answer: Henry's law.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: If the partial pressure of nitrogen in the lungs becomes four times larger, by what factor does its mole fraction in blood change (temperature constant)?
subqs.answer: It becomes four times larger, since x = p/K_H.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why do nitrogen bubbles form when the diver surfaces quickly?
subqs.answer: The pressure falls rapidly, lowering the solubility of nitrogen, so the excess dissolved nitrogen comes out of solution as bubbles (bends).

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: What would happen if a diver used pure oxygen instead of helium-diluted air at great depths? Evaluate.
subqs.answer: High dissolved oxygen concentrations become toxic, so pure oxygen at high pressure is dangerous; helium-diluted mixtures reduce both nitrogen and oxygen toxicity.

questions.q: In a solution of a non-volatile solid in a volatile liquid, the vapour pressure of the solution is due to:
questions.hint: Only volatile components contribute to vapour pressure; the non-volatile solute does not.
questions.whyTier: It is a direct conceptual point from NCERT section 1.4.
opts: C. Both solute and solvent equally

questions.q: Liquid solutions are formed when the ________ is a liquid.
questions.answer: solvent
questions.whyTier: It completes the opening statement of NCERT section 1.4.

questions.q: In a liquid solution, the solute must always be volatile.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: The solute may be a gas, a liquid or a solid, and may or may not be volatile.
questions.whyTier: It tests a subtle point mentioned in passing in the text.

questions.q: Match the type of liquid solution with its example.
questions.whyTier: Examples are taken from NCERT.

questions.q: Identify the odd mixture with respect to the volatility of its components.
questions.answer: Glucose + water
questions.hint: Glucose is non-volatile; in the other mixtures both components are volatile.
questions.whyTier: It is a classification task.

questions.q: What is meant by the vapour pressure of a liquid?
questions.answer: It is the pressure exerted by the vapour of a liquid in equilibrium with the liquid phase at a given temperature.
questions.whyTier: It is a basic definition used throughout the chapter.

questions.q: Name the two kinds of binary liquid solutions whose vapour pressures are discussed in this chapter, and give one example of each.
questions.answer: (i) Solutions of liquids in liquids, e.g. benzene and toluene, where both components may be volatile. (ii) Solutions of solids in liquids, e.g. glucose in water, where the solute is non-volatile.
questions.whyTier: It recalls the NCERT classification directly.

questions.q: Case Study: Room fresheners
questions.passage: A room freshener contains a mixture of two volatile liquids that slowly evaporate and spread fragrance. A second product is a gel made by dissolving a non-volatile solid in a little water. Both are kept in closed containers before use. When opened, the liquid freshener smells strong at once, while the gel releases mostly water vapour.
questions.whyTier: It applies the concept to a scenario not discussed in NCERT, an open-ended Tier 2 task.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Which product is a solution of a liquid in a liquid?
subqs.answer: The liquid room freshener containing two volatile liquids.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: In the gel, which component contributes to the vapour pressure?
subqs.answer: Only the solvent, water, since the solid solute is non-volatile.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why does a closed container of the liquid freshener develop a vapour pressure above the liquid?
subqs.answer: Molecules of both volatile liquids evaporate until an equilibrium is set up between the vapour phase and the liquid phase.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: Predict what happens to the smell if one of the two liquids in the freshener were replaced by a non-volatile liquid.
subqs.answer: The fragrance would come only from the remaining volatile component and would be weaker, because the non-volatile liquid does not contribute to the vapour.

questions.q: For an ideal solution of two volatile liquids, the total vapour pressure varies with the mole fraction of component 2 as:
questions.hint: p_total = p₁⁰ + (p₂⁰ − p₁⁰) x₂, which is a straight-line relation.
questions.whyTier: It is a conclusion drawn directly from NCERT equation 1.16.

questions.q: According to Raoult's law, for a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component is directly proportional to its ________ present in solution.
questions.answer: mole fraction
questions.whyTier: It completes the NCERT statement of Raoult's law.

questions.q: At equilibrium, the vapour phase above a solution of two volatile liquids is always richer in the more volatile component.
questions.answer: True
questions.hint: This is the NCERT conclusion from Example 1.5.
questions.whyTier: It is a key conclusion highlighted in bold in NCERT.

questions.whyTier: All equations appear directly in NCERT section 1.4.1.
