questions.whyTier: It is a classification task across sections.

questions.q: State Raoult's law for a solution of volatile liquids.
questions.answer: For a solution of volatile liquids, the partial vapour pressure of each component is directly proportional to its mole fraction present in the solution.
questions.whyTier: It is a law statement directly from NCERT.

questions.q: Two volatile liquids A and B (p_A⁰ < p_B⁰) form an ideal solution. Explain why the vapour in equilibrium with the solution contains a larger mole fraction of B than the liquid does.
questions.answer: 1. By Raoult's law, p_B = x_B p_B⁰ and p_A = x_A p_A⁰.\n2. By Dalton's law, y_B = p_B/p_total = x_B p_B⁰/(x_A p_A⁰ + x_B p_B⁰).\n3. Since p_B⁰ > p_A⁰, the denominator is less than p_B⁰, so y_B > x_B. Hence the vapour is richer in the more volatile component B.
questions.whyTier: It explains a highlighted NCERT conclusion.

questions.q: Pure liquids A and B have vapour pressures of 300 mm Hg and 800 mm Hg respectively at 330 K. Calculate the total vapour pressure of an ideal solution in which the mole fraction of A is 0.4.
questions.answer:
Given: p_A⁰ = 300 mm Hg, p_B⁰ = 800 mm Hg, x_A = 0.4, x_B = 0.6.
Formula: p_total = x_A p_A⁰ + x_B p_B⁰.
Substitution: p_total = 0.4 × 300 + 0.6 × 800 = 120 + 480 mm Hg.
Answer: p_total = 600 mm Hg.
questions.whyTier: It applies Raoult's and Dalton's laws with new values.

questions.q: At 350 K, the vapour pressures of pure benzene and pure toluene are 700 mm Hg and 280 mm Hg respectively. A solution is made from 39 g of benzene and 46 g of toluene. Assuming ideal behaviour, calculate (a) the partial pressures of both components, (b) the total vapour pressure and (c) the mole fraction of benzene in the vapour phase.
questions.answer:
Given: p_B⁰ = 700 mm Hg, p_T⁰ = 280 mm Hg; M(C₆H₆) = 78 g mol⁻¹, M(C₇H₈) = 92 g mol⁻¹.
Moles: benzene = 39/78 = 0.50 mol; toluene = 46/92 = 0.50 mol; so x_B = x_T = 0.50.
(a) p_B = x_B p_B⁰ = 0.50 × 700 = 350 mm Hg; p_T = 0.50 × 280 = 140 mm Hg.
(b) p_total = 350 + 140 = 490 mm Hg.
(c) y_B = p_B/p_total = 350/490 = 0.714.
Answer: 350 mm Hg and 140 mm Hg; 490 mm Hg; y(benzene) = 0.714, showing the vapour is richer in the more volatile benzene.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT-style multi-step numerical modelled on Example 1.5.
keyPoints: p_B = 350 mm Hg, p_T = 140 mm Hg

questions.q: Starting from Raoult's law and Dalton's law of partial pressures, derive the expression p_total = p₁⁰ + (p₂⁰ − p₁⁰) x₂ for an ideal binary solution of volatile liquids, and state the conclusions that follow from it.
questions.answer:
1. Raoult's law for component 1: p₁ = x₁ p₁⁰.
2. Raoult's law for component 2: p₂ = x₂ p₂⁰.
3. Dalton's law: p_total = p₁ + p₂ = x₁ p₁⁰ + x₂ p₂⁰.
4. For a binary solution x₁ = 1 − x₂, so p_total = (1 − x₂) p₁⁰ + x₂ p₂⁰.
5. Rearranging: p_total = p₁⁰ + (p₂⁰ − p₁⁰) x₂.
Conclusions: (i) total vapour pressure can be related to the mole fraction of any one component; (ii) it varies linearly with x₂; (iii) depending on p₁⁰ and p₂⁰ it increases or decreases with the mole fraction of component 1. Condition: valid only for ideal solutions obeying Raoult's law.
questions.whyTier: This derivation (equations 1.14–1.16) is in the NCERT text and syllabus.
keyPoints: p₁ = x₁ p₁⁰ and p₂ = x₂ p₂⁰
Linear in x₂; valid for ideal solutions

questions.q: Sketch a graph of p₁, p₂ and p_total against mole fraction (x₁ from 1 to 0, x₂ from 0 to 1) for an ideal solution, and label the intercepts.
questions.answer: p₁ is a straight line falling from p₁⁰ (at x₁ = 1) to zero (at x₁ = 0). p₂ is a straight line rising from zero (at x₂ = 0) to p₂⁰ (at x₂ = 1). p_total is a straight line joining p₁⁰ and p₂⁰; its minimum is p₁⁰ and maximum is p₂⁰ when component 1 is less volatile.
questions.whyTier: It reproduces NCERT Fig. 1.3, a commonly examined diagram.

questions.q: Case Study: Separating a solvent mixture
questions.passage: A paint factory recovers a used mixture of benzene and toluene, which behaves almost ideally. Engineers heat the mixture in a closed still and collect the vapour above the liquid. They notice that the condensed vapour contains a larger share of benzene than the original liquid. Repeating the process several times gives almost pure benzene.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Which law gives the partial vapour pressure of each component in the still?
subqs.answer: Raoult's law (pᵢ = xᵢ pᵢ⁰).

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: If x(benzene) = 0.6 in the liquid and p⁰(benzene) = 0.30 bar, what is the partial pressure of benzene?

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why is the condensed vapour richer in benzene?
subqs.answer: Benzene is more volatile (higher p⁰), so its partial pressure, and hence its mole fraction in the vapour (y = p/p_total), is greater than in the liquid.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: Would this process work as well if the two liquids had equal vapour pressures? Evaluate.
subqs.answer: No. With equal p⁰ values, the vapour would have the same composition as the liquid, so repeated evaporation and condensation would give no enrichment.

questions.q: Raoult's law becomes a special case of Henry's law when:
questions.hint: Both laws have the form p = constant × x; they coincide when K_H equals the vapour pressure of the pure component.
questions.whyTier: It is stated directly in NCERT section 1.4.2.

questions.q: In Henry's law the proportionality constant is K_H, whereas in Raoult's law it is the ________ of the pure component.
questions.answer: vapour pressure
questions.whyTier: It completes the NCERT comparison of the two laws.

questions.q: Henry's law and Raoult's law both state that the partial pressure of a volatile component is directly proportional to its mole fraction in the solution.
questions.answer: True
questions.hint: They differ only in the proportionality constant (K_H versus p⁰).
questions.whyTier: It tests the central NCERT idea of this section.

questions.q: Match the items related to Raoult's and Henry's laws.
questions.whyTier: All points come from NCERT section 1.4.2.

pairs.L: Component so volatile it exists as a gas

pairs.R: Raoult's law becomes a special case of Henry's law

questions.q: Pick the relation that is NOT of the form 'partial pressure ∝ mole fraction'.
questions.answer: ΔT_b = K_b m
questions.hint: It relates boiling-point elevation to molality, not partial pressure to mole fraction.
questions.whyTier: It requires comparing laws across sections.

questions.q: Under what condition does Raoult's law become a special case of Henry's law?
questions.answer: When the Henry's law constant K_H becomes equal to the vapour pressure of the pure component, p₁⁰.
questions.whyTier: It is a direct NCERT statement.

questions.q: Give one similarity and one difference between Raoult's law and Henry's law.
questions.answer: Similarity: both state that the partial pressure of a volatile component is directly proportional to its mole fraction in solution. Difference: the proportionality constant is the pure-component vapour pressure p⁰ in Raoult's law but K_H (which depends on the gas and solvent) in Henry's law.
questions.whyTier: Comparing two laws is a reasoning task of moderate exam likelihood.

questions.q: A volatile liquid behaves so that its K_H equals its pure vapour pressure, 0.40 bar, at a given temperature. Calculate (a) its partial pressure when its mole fraction is 0.25 and (b) its mole fraction when its partial pressure is 0.30 bar.
questions.answer:
Given: K_H = p⁰ = 0.40 bar.
Formula: p = K_H x (= x p⁰).
(a) p = 0.40 bar × 0.25 = 0.10 bar.
(b) x = p/K_H = 0.30 bar / 0.40 bar = 0.75.
Answer: 0.10 bar; 0.75.
questions.whyTier: It is a student-constructed application of the two laws.

questions.q: Both Raoult's law and Henry's law give straight-line graphs of partial pressure versus mole fraction. What does the slope represent in each case?
questions.answer: For Raoult's law the slope is the vapour pressure of the pure component (p⁰); for Henry's law the slope is the Henry's law constant K_H. Both lines pass through the origin.
questions.whyTier: It requires interpreting graphs of both laws together.

questions.q: Case Study: One law or two?
questions.passage: A student studies two systems at the same temperature: carbon dioxide dissolved in water under pressure, and ethanol dissolved in water. In both, she finds that the partial pressure of the dissolved component rises in proportion to its mole fraction. For CO₂ the proportionality constant is far larger than for ethanol. Her teacher says both observations are really described by the same type of law.
questions.whyTier: It applies the comparison to a new scenario, an open-ended Tier 2 task.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Which law is normally used for CO₂ in water?
subqs.answer: Henry's law.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: If K_H for CO₂ is 1.67 kbar, what partial pressure of CO₂ gives a mole fraction of 6.0 × 10⁻⁴?

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why does the teacher say both systems follow the same type of law?
subqs.answer: In both, partial pressure is directly proportional to mole fraction (p = constant × x); only the constant differs.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: When would ethanol's constant match the Raoult's law constant? Explain.
subqs.answer: When the proportionality constant equals the vapour pressure of pure ethanol, p⁰; then Henry's law reduces to Raoult's law.

questions.q: The vapour pressure of a solvent is lowered on adding a non-volatile solute mainly because:
questions.hint: Solute particles occupy part of the surface, so fewer solvent molecules can escape.
questions.whyTier: It is the NCERT explanation of vapour-pressure lowering (Fig. 1.4).
opts: A. The solute reacts chemically with the solvent
B. The fraction of the surface covered by solvent molecules is reduced
C. The boiling point of the solvent decreases
D. The temperature of the solution falls

questions.q: For a solution of a non-volatile solute, p₁ = x₁ p₁⁰, i.e. the vapour pressure of the solution is proportional to the mole fraction of the ________.
questions.answer: solvent
questions.whyTier: It completes NCERT equation 1.20.

questions.q: Adding 1.0 mol of sucrose to 1 kg of water lowers its vapour pressure by nearly the same amount as adding 1.0 mol of urea at the same temperature.
questions.answer: True
questions.hint: The lowering depends on the quantity of solute particles, not their nature.
questions.whyTier: It is a direct NCERT statement.

questions.q: Match each item about a solution of a non-volatile solute with its description.
questions.whyTier: All points come from NCERT Figs. 1.4 and 1.5.

pairs.R: Shared between solute and solvent particles
Does not contribute to vapour pressure

questions.q: Which solute, when added to water, is the odd one out in this group?
questions.answer: Ethanol
questions.hint: Ethanol is volatile and contributes to vapour pressure; the others are non-volatile solids.
questions.whyTier: It is a classification task.

questions.q: Why is the vapour pressure of an aqueous glucose solution lower than that of pure water at the same temperature?
questions.answer: Glucose particles occupy part of the surface, so fewer water molecules escape into the vapour phase.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT 'explain why' question.

questions.q: Explain, at the molecular level, why the vapour pressure of a solvent decreases when a non-volatile solute is dissolved in it.
questions.answer: 1. In a pure liquid, the entire surface is occupied by solvent molecules, which escape into the vapour and set up vapour pressure.\n2. In a solution, non-volatile solute particles also occupy part of the surface, reducing the fraction of surface covered by solvent molecules.\n3. Hence fewer solvent molecules escape per unit time, and the vapour pressure at equilibrium is lower than that of the pure solvent.
questions.whyTier: The explanation with Fig. 1.4 is standard NCERT content.

questions.q: The vapour pressure of pure water at 298 K is 23.8 mm Hg. Calculate the vapour pressure of a solution containing 0.5 mol of a non-volatile solute in 9.5 mol of water at this temperature.
questions.answer:
Given: p₁⁰ = 23.8 mm Hg; n₂ = 0.5 mol, n₁ = 9.5 mol.
Formula: p₁ = x₁ p₁⁰, with x₁ = n₁/(n₁ + n₂).
Substitution: x₁ = 9.5/10.0 = 0.95; p₁ = 0.95 × 23.8 mm Hg.
Answer: p₁ = 22.61 mm Hg.
questions.whyTier: It applies equation 1.20 with new values.

questions.q: Sketch how the vapour pressure of a solution of a non-volatile solute varies with the mole fraction of the solvent, and state what the graph shows.
questions.answer: The graph is a straight line from zero (at x₁ = 0) to p₁⁰ (at x₁ = 1). It shows that the vapour pressure is directly proportional to the mole fraction of the solvent, as Raoult's law predicts.
questions.whyTier: It reproduces NCERT Fig. 1.5.

questions.q: Case Study: Why sea water evaporates slowly
questions.passage: Two identical open trays, one filled with fresh water and the other with sea water, are left in the sun at a salt pan. After a day, the level of fresh water has fallen more than that of sea water. Sea water contains dissolved salts that do not evaporate. The workers say the salts 'hold back' the water.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Which liquid has the lower vapour pressure at the same temperature?
subqs.answer: Sea water.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: If the mole fraction of water in sea water is 0.98 and p⁰(water) is 30 mm Hg, what is the vapour pressure of sea water?

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Explain the workers' idea that salts 'hold back' the water.
subqs.answer: Dissolved salt particles occupy part of the surface, reducing the number of water molecules that can escape, so evaporation is slower.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: What would happen to the evaporation rate as the sea water becomes more concentrated over the day?
subqs.answer: It would decrease further, because the mole fraction of water falls, lowering its vapour pressure even more.

questions.q: Liquid–liquid solutions are classified as ideal or non-ideal on the basis of:
questions.hint: Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration.
questions.whyTier: It is a direct NCERT statement.

questions.q: Solutions that obey Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration are called ________ solutions.
questions.answer: ideal
questions.whyTier: It is an examinable NCERT definition.

questions.q: All liquid–liquid solutions obey Raoult's law at every composition.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: Only ideal solutions do; non-ideal solutions show positive or negative deviations.
questions.whyTier: It targets a basic misconception.

questions.q: Match each term with its meaning.
questions.whyTier: All definitions are from NCERT section 1.5.

pairs.R: Obeys Raoult's law at all compositions
Vapour pressure higher than predicted by Raoult's law
Vapour pressure lower than predicted by Raoult's law

questions.q: Identify the pair that does not behave nearly ideally.
questions.answer: Phenol + aniline
questions.hint: Phenol and aniline form strong A–B hydrogen bonds and show negative deviation.
questions.whyTier: It is a sorting task based on NCERT examples.

questions.q: On what basis are liquid–liquid solutions classified as ideal or non-ideal?
questions.answer: On the basis of whether or not they obey Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration.
questions.whyTier: It is a direct NCERT statement.

questions.q: Distinguish between an ideal and a non-ideal solution in terms of Raoult's law, giving one example of each.
questions.answer: An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration, e.g. benzene and toluene. A non-ideal solution does not obey Raoult's law over the entire range; its vapour pressure is higher or lower than predicted, e.g. chloroform and acetone.
questions.whyTier: It is a standard 2-mark CBSE comparison.

questions.q: On the same axes, sketch the total vapour pressure against composition for (i) an ideal solution and (ii) a solution showing positive deviation from Raoult's law. Explain the difference.
questions.answer: (i) For the ideal solution, p_total is a straight line joining p₁⁰ and p₂⁰. (ii) For positive deviation, the curve lies above this straight line at intermediate compositions. The difference arises because weaker A–B interactions let molecules escape more easily, raising the vapour pressure above the Raoult's law value.
questions.whyTier: It requires comparing two graphs, an extended reasoning task.

questions.q: Case Study: Mixing solvents in the laboratory
questions.passage: A technician mixes n-hexane with n-heptane and notices no temperature change, and the total volume equals the sum of the volumes taken. She then mixes chloroform with acetone and finds that the mixture warms up and its vapour pressure is lower than expected. She records both results for the lab manual.
questions.whyTier: It applies the classification to a new laboratory scenario.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Which mixture behaves as an ideal solution?
subqs.answer: n-hexane and n-heptane.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: If equimolar chloroform–acetone is predicted by Raoult's law to have a vapour pressure of 300 mm Hg, is the observed value higher or lower than 300 mm Hg?
subqs.answer: Lower than 300 mm Hg (negative deviation).

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why does the chloroform–acetone mixture warm up?
subqs.answer: New, stronger A–B interactions (hydrogen bonding) form, so heat is released (Δ_mix H < 0).

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: Would you expect the hexane–heptane mixture to change temperature if mixed in different proportions? Explain.
subqs.answer: No. It is nearly ideal at all compositions, with Δ_mix H = 0 because A–A, B–B and A–B interactions are similar.

questions.q: For an ideal solution, which of the following is correct?
questions.hint: No heat is absorbed or evolved and there is no volume change on mixing.
questions.whyTier: It tests NCERT equation 1.21 directly.
opts: A. Δ_mix H = 0 and Δ_mix V = 0
B. Δ_mix H > 0 and Δ_mix V > 0
C. Δ_mix H < 0 and Δ_mix V < 0
D. Δ_mix H = 0 and Δ_mix V > 0

questions.q: An ideal solution forms when the A–A and B–B intermolecular attractive forces are nearly equal to the ________ interactions.
questions.answer: A–B
questions.whyTier: It is the NCERT molecular-level condition for ideality.

questions.q: When two liquids forming an ideal solution are mixed, the volume of the solution equals the sum of the volumes of the two components.
questions.answer: True
questions.hint: Δ_mix V = 0 for an ideal solution.
questions.whyTier: It is a stated NCERT property of ideal solutions.

questions.q: Match each property with its value or example for an ideal solution.
questions.whyTier: All points come directly from NCERT section 1.5.1.

questions.q: Identify the pair that does NOT form a nearly ideal solution.
questions.answer: Ethanol and acetone
questions.hint: Ethanol–acetone shows positive deviation because acetone breaks the hydrogen bonds of ethanol.
questions.whyTier: It requires sorting examples across subsections.

questions.q: What is the value of the enthalpy of mixing for an ideal solution?
questions.answer: Zero (Δ_mix H = 0); no heat is absorbed or evolved on mixing.
questions.whyTier: It recalls an NCERT property.

questions.q: Explain the ideal behaviour of a solution of two components A and B at the molecular level.
questions.answer: 1. In pure A and pure B, the intermolecular attractions are of types A–A and B–B.\n2. In the solution, A–B interactions are also present.\n3. If the A–B attractions are nearly equal to the A–A and B–B attractions, mixing causes no change in energy or volume (Δ_mix H = 0, Δ_mix V = 0), and each component obeys Raoult's law, so the solution is ideal.
questions.whyTier: It is the NCERT molecular explanation and a common 3-mark question.

questions.q: Liquids X (p⁰ = 120 mm Hg) and Y (p⁰ = 80 mm Hg) form an ideal solution with a total vapour pressure of 100 mm Hg at a certain temperature. Find the mole fraction of X in the liquid and in the vapour.
questions.answer:
Given: p_X⁰ = 120 mm Hg, p_Y⁰ = 80 mm Hg, p_total = 100 mm Hg.
Formula: p_total = p_Y⁰ + (p_X⁰ − p_Y⁰) x_X; y_X = x_X p_X⁰/p_total.
Substitution: 100 = 80 + 40 x_X, so x_X = 0.50; p_X = 0.50 × 120 = 60 mm Hg; y_X = 60/100 = 0.60.
Answer: x_X = 0.50 in the liquid; y_X = 0.60 in the vapour.
questions.whyTier: It requires an extra step (finding x from p_total) beyond the NCERT examples.

questions.q: Case Study: Blending petrol fractions
questions.passage: In a refinery, n-hexane and n-heptane obtained from crude oil are blended to make a fuel component. Engineers find that blending them neither warms nor cools the tank, and 600 L of hexane mixed with 400 L of heptane gives exactly 1000 L. The vapour pressure of every blend matches the value calculated from Raoult's law.
questions.whyTier: It applies the concept to an industrial scenario.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: What type of solution do these two hydrocarbons form?
subqs.answer: An (almost) ideal solution.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: What is Δ_mix V for this blend? Use the data given.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why does mixing produce no temperature change?
subqs.answer: The A–B interactions are nearly equal to A–A and B–B interactions, so Δ_mix H = 0.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: Would you expect the same behaviour if ethanol were blended with the hexane? Explain.
subqs.answer: No. Ethanol is hydrogen bonded; hexane would break these bonds, weakening interactions, so the mixture would deviate positively from Raoult's law with Δ_mix H > 0.

questions.q: A mixture of chloroform and acetone shows:
questions.hint: Chloroform forms a hydrogen bond with acetone, so A–B interactions are stronger.
questions.whyTier: It is a standard NCERT example.
opts: A. Positive deviation from Raoult's law
B. Negative deviation from Raoult's law
D. No vapour pressure at all

questions.q: Solutions showing a large positive deviation from Raoult's law form ________ boiling azeotropes.
questions.answer: minimum
questions.whyTier: It completes an NCERT statement.

questions.q: An azeotrope can be separated into its pure components by fractional distillation.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: An azeotrope has the same composition in liquid and vapour, so distillation cannot separate it.
questions.whyTier: It targets a frequently tested misconception.

questions.q: Match each mixture with its behaviour.
questions.whyTier: All examples appear in NCERT section 1.5.2.

questions.q: Which mixture is the odd one out with respect to the type of deviation from Raoult's law?
questions.answer: Chloroform + acetone
questions.hint: It shows negative deviation; the other three show positive deviation.
questions.whyTier: It is a classification task requiring reasoning about interactions.

questions.q: What is an azeotrope?
questions.answer: An azeotrope is a binary mixture having the same composition in the liquid and vapour phases, which boils at a constant temperature.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT definition.

questions.q: Explain why a mixture of chloroform and acetone shows negative deviation from Raoult's law.
questions.answer: 1. In the mixture, the hydrogen of chloroform forms a hydrogen bond with the oxygen of acetone.\n2. These A–B interactions are stronger than the A–A and B–B interactions in the pure liquids.\n3. Molecules therefore escape less easily, the escaping tendency falls, and the vapour pressure is lower than predicted by Raoult's law: a negative deviation.
questions.whyTier: It is a standard NCERT explanation.

questions.q: Pure liquids A and B have vapour pressures of 400 mm Hg and 600 mm Hg. An equimolar solution of A and B has an observed total vapour pressure of 560 mm Hg. Predict the ideal value, identify the type of deviation and state the sign of Δ_mix H.
questions.answer:
Given: p_A⁰ = 400 mm Hg, p_B⁰ = 600 mm Hg, x_A = x_B = 0.5, observed p = 560 mm Hg.
Formula: p_ideal = x_A p_A⁰ + x_B p_B⁰.
Substitution: p_ideal = 0.5 × 400 + 0.5 × 600 = 500 mm Hg.
Answer: Observed 560 mm Hg > 500 mm Hg, so the solution shows positive deviation; A–B interactions are weaker, so mixing is endothermic (Δ_mix H > 0).
questions.whyTier: It combines Raoult's law with deviation analysis, a two-concept problem.

questions.q: Draw labelled vapour pressure–composition diagrams for a solution showing (a) positive deviation and (b) negative deviation from Raoult's law.
questions.answer: (a) Positive deviation: the p₁, p₂ and p_total curves all lie above the straight Raoult's law lines, with p_total bulging upward at intermediate compositions. (b) Negative deviation: the curves lie below the Raoult's law lines, with p_total sagging downward. Axes: vapour pressure on the y-axis; x₁ (1→0) and x₂ (0→1) on the x-axis.
questions.whyTier: It reproduces NCERT Fig. 1.6, a frequently examined diagram.

questions.q: Case Study: Why fuel ethanol needs extra drying
questions.passage: A distillery ferments sugar and distils the ethanol–water mixture to make fuel ethanol. However hard they try, the distillate never goes beyond about 95% ethanol by volume. At this composition, the liquid and the vapour have the same composition. The company must use other methods to remove the last 5% of water.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: What name is given to a mixture whose liquid and vapour have the same composition?
subqs.answer: An azeotrope.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: Is this a minimum or a maximum boiling azeotrope?
subqs.answer: A minimum boiling azeotrope.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why can't simple fractional distillation take the ethanol beyond 95%?
subqs.answer: At the azeotropic composition the vapour has the same composition as the liquid, so further distillation produces no enrichment.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: What type of deviation from Raoult's law causes this azeotrope, and why?
subqs.answer: A large positive deviation, because ethanol–water A–B interactions are weaker than the hydrogen-bonded interactions in the pure liquids.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a colligative property?
questions.hint: The relative lowering of vapour pressure is colligative; the vapour pressure itself depends on the nature of the solvent.
questions.whyTier: Identifying colligative properties is a frequently asked NCERT-based question.
opts: C. Vapour pressure of the solution

questions.q: Colligative properties depend on the ________ of solute particles, irrespective of their nature, relative to the total number of particles in the solution.
questions.answer: number
questions.whyTier: It completes the NCERT definition highlighted in bold.

questions.q: A 0.1 m aqueous solution of glucose and a 0.1 m aqueous solution of urea show nearly the same depression in freezing point.
questions.answer: True
questions.hint: Both are non-electrolytes giving the same number of solute particles per kg of solvent.
questions.whyTier: It tests the core idea of colligative properties.

questions.q: Match each colligative property with its mathematical expression.
questions.whyTier: All four formulas appear directly in the NCERT text.

questions.q: Identify the property that does NOT belong to the group.
questions.answer: Colour of the solution
questions.hint: Colour depends on the nature of the solute; the others depend only on the number of solute particles.
questions.whyTier: It is a classification task.

questions.q: What is the origin of the word 'colligative'?
questions.answer: From Latin: 'co' means together and 'ligare' means to bind.
questions.whyTier: It tests background information, a Tier 2 feature.

questions.q: List the four colligative properties of a solution and state on what they depend.
questions.answer: (1) Relative lowering of vapour pressure, (2) elevation of boiling point, (3) depression of freezing point and (4) osmotic pressure. They depend only on the number of solute particles relative to the total number of particles, not on the nature of the solute.
questions.whyTier: It recalls a central NCERT list.

questions.q: Case Study: Salt on icy roads
questions.passage: In cold countries, road workers spread salt on icy roads; the ice melts even below 0 °C. In summer, cooks notice that salted water boils a little above 100 °C. Doctors use isotonic saline for drips so that blood cells keep their normal shape. All three effects depend on how many particles are dissolved, not on what they are.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Name the colligative property used by the road workers.
subqs.answer: Depression of freezing point.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: If 1 mol of glucose or 1 mol of urea were dissolved in 1 kg of water, which would lower the freezing point more?
subqs.answer: Neither; both give the same number of particles and hence about the same depression.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why does salted water boil above 100 °C?
subqs.answer: The dissolved salt lowers the vapour pressure of water, so a higher temperature is needed for it to reach atmospheric pressure (elevation of boiling point).

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: What would happen to blood cells if pure water were given in a drip instead of saline? Explain.
subqs.answer: Water would enter the cells by osmosis and they would swell and may burst, because pure water is hypotonic to the cell fluid.

questions.q: The relative lowering of vapour pressure of a solution containing a non-volatile solute is equal to:
questions.hint: (p₁⁰ − p₁)/p₁⁰ = x₂.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT result highlighted in bold.
opts: A. The mole fraction of the solvent
B. The mole fraction of the solute
C. The molality of the solution
D. The molarity of the solution

questions.q: (p₁⁰ − p₁)/p₁⁰ = ________, where the symbol is the mole fraction of the solute.
questions.answer: x₂
questions.whyTier: It completes NCERT equation 1.25.

questions.q: The relative lowering of vapour pressure depends on the chemical nature of the non-volatile solute.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: It depends only on the concentration (number) of solute particles.
questions.whyTier: It targets a misconception about colligative properties.

questions.q: Match each quantity with its expression.
questions.whyTier: All relations are NCERT equations 1.23–1.28.

questions.q: Identify the expression that is NOT equal to the relative lowering of vapour pressure.
questions.answer: K_H
questions.hint: K_H is Henry's law constant; the others all equal the relative lowering of vapour pressure.
questions.whyTier: It requires recognising equivalent forms.

questions.q: Why is the relative lowering of vapour pressure a colligative property?
questions.answer: Because it is equal to the mole fraction of the solute, which depends only on the number of solute particles and not on their nature.
questions.whyTier: It is a direct conceptual question from NCERT.

questions.q: Derive an expression for the molar mass of a non-volatile solute from the relative lowering of vapour pressure of its dilute solution.
questions.answer:
1. By Raoult's law for the solvent, p₁ = x₁ p₁⁰, so Δp₁ = p₁⁰ − p₁ = p₁⁰(1 − x₁) = x₂ p₁⁰.
2. Hence the relative lowering is (p₁⁰ − p₁)/p₁⁰ = x₂ = n₂/(n₁ + n₂).
3. For a dilute solution n₂ << n₁, so (p₁⁰ − p₁)/p₁⁰ ≈ n₂/n₁.
4. Substitute n₂ = w₂/M₂ and n₁ = w₁/M₁: (p₁⁰ − p₁)/p₁⁰ = (w₂ × M₁)/(M₂ × w₁).
5. Rearranging: M₂ = (w₂ × M₁ × p₁⁰)/(w₁ × (p₁⁰ − p₁)).
Conditions: valid for dilute solutions of non-volatile, non-electrolyte solutes that neither associate nor dissociate.
questions.whyTier: This derivation (equations 1.22–1.28) is part of the NCERT text.

questions.q: The vapour pressure of pure water at 293 K is 17.5 mm Hg. Calculate the vapour pressure of a solution made by dissolving 18 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) in 178.2 g of water at this temperature.
questions.answer:
Given: p₁⁰ = 17.5 mm Hg; w₂ = 18 g, M₂ = 180 g mol⁻¹; w₁ = 178.2 g, M₁ = 18 g mol⁻¹.
Formula: (p₁⁰ − p₁)/p₁⁰ = x₂.
Substitution: n₂ = 18/180 = 0.10 mol; n₁ = 178.2/18 = 9.90 mol; x₂ = 0.10/10.00 = 0.010.
p₁ = p₁⁰(1 − x₂) = 17.5 × 0.990 = 17.325 mm Hg.
Answer: p₁ ≈ 17.33 mm Hg.
questions.whyTier: It applies the RLVP formula with new values.

questions.q: 2.0 g of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute is dissolved in 50 g of benzene (M = 78 g mol⁻¹). The vapour pressure of benzene falls from 0.650 bar to 0.640 bar at the same temperature. Calculate the molar mass of the solute.
questions.answer:
Given: w₂ = 2.0 g, w₁ = 50 g, M₁ = 78 g mol⁻¹, p₁⁰ = 0.650 bar, p₁ = 0.640 bar.
Step 1: Relative lowering = (0.650 − 0.640)/0.650 = 0.010/0.650 = 0.01538.
Step 2: Formula: (p₁⁰ − p₁)/p₁⁰ = (w₂ × M₁)/(M₂ × w₁).
Step 3: M₂ = (w₂ × M₁)/(w₁ × 0.01538) = (2.0 g × 78 g mol⁻¹)/(50 g × 0.01538).
Step 4: M₂ = 156/0.769 g mol⁻¹ = 202.8 g mol⁻¹.
Answer: Molar mass of the solute ≈ 203 g mol⁻¹.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT-style molar-mass numerical (like Example 1.6) with new values.

questions.q: Sketch a graph of relative lowering of vapour pressure (y-axis) against mole fraction of a non-volatile solute (x-axis) for dilute solutions. What is its slope?
questions.answer: The graph is a straight line through the origin with slope equal to 1, because the relative lowering of vapour pressure equals x₂.
questions.whyTier: It interprets the RLVP relation graphically, beyond the NCERT figures.

questions.q: Case Study: Sugar syrup in the kitchen
questions.passage: A confectioner keeps two open bowls in a warm kitchen: one with plain water and one with thick sugar syrup. After a few hours, the water bowl has lost noticeably more liquid than the syrup bowl. Sugar is non-volatile and does not evaporate. The confectioner measures that the syrup's vapour pressure is 10% lower than that of water at the same temperature.
questions.whyTier: It applies the concept to a new everyday scenario.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Name the colligative property shown by the syrup.
subqs.answer: Relative lowering of vapour pressure.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: From the data, what is the mole fraction of sugar in the syrup?
subqs.answer: Relative lowering = 0.10, so x(sugar) = 0.10.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why does the syrup lose water more slowly?
subqs.answer: Its vapour pressure is lower because sugar particles reduce the fraction of the surface covered by water molecules, so fewer water molecules escape.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: If the confectioner used an equal number of moles of salt (NaCl) instead of sugar, would the lowering be the same? Evaluate.
subqs.answer: No, it would be larger, because NaCl dissociates into two ions, roughly doubling the number of solute particles.

questions.q: The SI-based unit of the molal elevation constant K_b is:
questions.hint: ΔT_b = K_b m, so K_b = ΔT_b/m has units K ÷ (mol kg⁻¹) = K kg mol⁻¹.
questions.whyTier: The unit of K_b is stated in NCERT and often asked.

questions.q: K_b is called the boiling point elevation constant, molal elevation constant or ________ constant.
questions.answer: ebullioscopic
questions.whyTier: It completes an NCERT definition.

questions.q: A solution of a non-volatile solute boils at a lower temperature than the pure solvent.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: Its vapour pressure is lower, so it must be heated to a higher temperature to boil.
questions.whyTier: It targets a common misconception.

questions.q: Match each boiling-point-elevation quantity with its expression.
questions.whyTier: All relations are NCERT equations 1.29–1.38.

questions.q: From Table 1.3, identify the value that does NOT belong to the group.
questions.answer: 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹ (water)
questions.hint: It is the K_f of water; the other three are K_b values.
questions.whyTier: It requires reading and classifying table data.

questions.q: Why does the boiling point of water rise when a non-volatile solute is dissolved in it?
questions.answer: The solute lowers the vapour pressure of water, so a higher temperature is needed for the vapour pressure to equal the atmospheric pressure.
questions.whyTier: It is a standard NCERT 'explain why' question.

questions.q: Starting from ΔT_b = K_b m, derive an expression for the molar mass M₂ of a non-volatile solute.
questions.answer:
Step 1: ΔT_b = K_b m (for dilute solutions).
Step 2: If w₂ g of solute of molar mass M₂ is dissolved in w₁ g of solvent, m = (w₂/M₂)/(w₁/1000) = (1000 × w₂)/(M₂ × w₁).
Step 3: Substituting, ΔT_b = (K_b × 1000 × w₂)/(M₂ × w₁), so M₂ = (1000 × w₂ × K_b)/(ΔT_b × w₁).
Condition: valid for dilute solutions of non-volatile solutes that do not associate or dissociate.
questions.whyTier: This derivation is given in NCERT (equations 1.31–1.33).

questions.q: Calculate the boiling point of a solution containing 9.0 g of glucose (M = 180 g mol⁻¹) in 250 g of water. (K_b for water = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹; boiling point of water = 373.15 K)
questions.answer:
Given: w₂ = 9.0 g, M₂ = 180 g mol⁻¹, w₁ = 250 g = 0.250 kg, K_b = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: ΔT_b = K_b m.
Substitution: n = 9.0/180 = 0.050 mol; m = 0.050/0.250 = 0.20 mol kg⁻¹; ΔT_b = 0.52 × 0.20 = 0.104 K.
Answer: T_b = 373.15 + 0.104 = 373.25 K.
questions.whyTier: It is a direct formula application with new values.

questions.q: 3.0 g of a non-volatile solute dissolved in 60 g of benzene raises its boiling point by 0.62 K. Given K_b for benzene = 2.53 K kg mol⁻¹ and the boiling point of benzene = 353.3 K, calculate (a) the molality of the solution, (b) the molar mass of the solute and (c) the boiling point of the solution.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT-style multi-step molar mass numerical (like Example 1.8).
keyPoints: M₂ = 1000 w₂ K_b/(ΔT_b w₁) = 204 g mol⁻¹

questions.q: Sketch the vapour pressure against temperature curves for a pure solvent and its solution with a non-volatile solute, and mark ΔT_b on the graph.
questions.answer: Both curves rise with temperature, and the solution curve lies below the solvent curve at every temperature. A horizontal line at 1.013 bar (atmospheric pressure) meets the solvent curve at T_b⁰ and the solution curve at a higher T_b. The gap T_b − T_b⁰ on the temperature axis is ΔT_b.
questions.whyTier: It reproduces NCERT Fig. 1.7.

questions.q: Case Study: Cooking with salted water
questions.passage: A cook adds a spoonful of salt to a large pot of water before boiling pasta. A thermometer shows that the salted water boils at about 100.2 °C instead of 100 °C. The cook believes salt makes the water 'hotter'. A chemistry student explains the real reason using colligative properties.
questions.whyTier: It applies the concept to an open-ended daily-life scenario.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Name the colligative property shown here.
subqs.answer: Elevation of boiling point.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: Taking K_b of water as 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹ and the observed ΔT_b as 0.2 K, what is the effective molality of solute particles?
subqs.answer: m = ΔT_b/K_b = 0.2/0.52 ≈ 0.38 mol kg⁻¹ of particles.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why does the salted water need a higher temperature to boil?
subqs.answer: Dissolved salt lowers the vapour pressure of water, so it must be heated more for its vapour pressure to reach atmospheric pressure.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: Evaluate the cook's claim that salt makes the water 'hotter' and speeds up cooking.
subqs.answer: The rise in boiling point (about 0.2 K) is very small, so the effect on cooking speed is negligible; salt mainly adds flavour.

questions.q: At the freezing point of a substance, the vapour pressure of its liquid phase is equal to the vapour pressure of its:
questions.hint: At the freezing point, solid and liquid are in dynamic equilibrium, so their vapour pressures are equal.
questions.whyTier: It is the NCERT definition of freezing point in terms of vapour pressure.
opts: C. Gaseous phase at the boiling point

questions.q: K_f is called the freezing point depression constant, molal depression constant or ________ constant.
questions.answer: cryoscopic
questions.whyTier: It completes an NCERT definition.

questions.q: The freezing point of a solution of a non-volatile solute is lower than that of the pure solvent.
questions.answer: True
questions.hint: ΔT_f = T_f⁰ − T_f is positive.
questions.whyTier: It is a central NCERT fact.

questions.q: Match each solvent with its K_f value (K kg mol⁻¹) from Table 1.3.
questions.whyTier: It uses NCERT Table 1.3 data.

questions.q: Which relation does NOT belong with the others?
questions.answer: p = K_H x
questions.hint: It is Henry's law; the others concern depression of freezing point.
questions.whyTier: It is a classification task across topics.
opts: K_f = R × M₁ × T_f² / (1000 × Δ_fus H)

questions.q: Define depression in freezing point.
questions.answer: It is the decrease in the freezing point of a solvent when a non-volatile solute is dissolved in it: ΔT_f = T_f⁰ − T_f.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT definition.

questions.q: Starting from ΔT_f = K_f m, derive the expression for the molar mass of a solute from freezing point depression data.
questions.answer:
Step 1: ΔT_f = K_f m.
Step 2: Molality m = (w₂/M₂)/(w₁/1000), so ΔT_f = (K_f × w₂/M₂)/(w₁/1000).
Step 3: ΔT_f = (K_f × w₂ × 1000)/(M₂ × w₁), giving M₂ = (K_f × w₂ × 1000)/(ΔT_f × w₁).
Condition: valid for dilute solutions; association or dissociation of the solute gives abnormal results.
questions.whyTier: This derivation (equations 1.35–1.36) is in NCERT.

questions.q: Calculate the freezing point of a solution made by dissolving 31 g of ethylene glycol (C₂H₆O₂, M = 62 g mol⁻¹) in 500 g of water. (K_f for water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹; freezing point of water = 273.15 K)
questions.answer:
Given: w₂ = 31 g, M₂ = 62 g mol⁻¹, w₁ = 500 g = 0.500 kg, K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: ΔT_f = K_f m.
Substitution: n = 31/62 = 0.50 mol; m = 0.50/0.500 = 1.00 mol kg⁻¹; ΔT_f = 1.86 × 1.00 = 1.86 K.
Answer: T_f = 273.15 − 1.86 = 271.29 K.
questions.whyTier: It is an antifreeze numerical with values different from Example 1.9.

questions.q: Using K_f = R × M₁ × T_f² / (1000 × Δ_fus H), calculate the cryoscopic constant of water. Given: Δ_fus H = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹, T_f = 273.15 K, M₁ = 18 g mol⁻¹, R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Compare the result with the value in Table 1.3.
questions.answer:
Given: R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, M₁ = 18 g mol⁻¹, T_f = 273.15 K, Δ_fus H = 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ = 6010 J mol⁻¹.
Step 1: T_f² = (273.15)² = 7.461 × 10⁴ K².
Step 2: Numerator = 8.314 × 18 × 7.461 × 10⁴ = 1.117 × 10⁷.
Step 3: Denominator = 1000 × 6010 = 6.010 × 10⁶.
Step 4: K_f = 1.117 × 10⁷ / 6.010 × 10⁶ = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.
Answer: K_f ≈ 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹, which matches the value for water in Table 1.3.
questions.whyTier: It uses an NCERT formula (1.37) in a way not worked out in the text.
keyPoints: Convert Δ_fus H to J mol⁻¹

questions.q: Draw a labelled diagram showing how the vapour pressure curves of a pure solvent (liquid), the solid solvent and a solution intersect, and mark ΔT_f.
questions.answer: The solid solvent curve is steep. The pure liquid solvent curve meets it at T_f⁰. The solution curve lies below the liquid solvent curve and meets the solid curve at a lower temperature T_f. The gap T_f⁰ − T_f on the temperature axis is ΔT_f.
questions.whyTier: It reproduces NCERT Fig. 1.8.

questions.q: Case Study: Antifreeze in car radiators
questions.passage: In Ladakh, winter temperatures fall well below 0 °C, and water in car radiators can freeze and crack the engine. Mechanics add ethylene glycol to the radiator water before winter. A 1 molal ethylene glycol solution freezes at about −1.86 °C, and higher concentrations protect against even colder nights. Ethylene glycol is chosen because it is non-volatile and mixes well with water.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: Name the colligative property that makes antifreeze work.
subqs.answer: Depression of freezing point.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: What molality of ethylene glycol is needed to lower the freezing point of water by 5.58 K (K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)?

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why is a non-volatile solute preferred as antifreeze?
subqs.answer: It does not evaporate from the hot radiator, so its concentration (and the freezing point lowering) is maintained.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: What would happen if methanol, which is volatile, were used instead during a long drive? Evaluate.
subqs.answer: Methanol would gradually evaporate from the hot engine, lowering its concentration, so the freezing point would rise and protection would be lost.

questions.q: The osmotic pressure π of a dilute solution of molarity C at temperature T is given by:
questions.hint: Osmotic pressure is proportional to molarity and temperature (equation 1.39).
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT formula commonly examined.

questions.q: Two solutions having the same osmotic pressure at a given temperature are called ________ solutions.
questions.answer: isotonic
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT definition in bold.

questions.q: During osmosis, solvent molecules flow through the semipermeable membrane from the more concentrated solution to the less concentrated solution.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: Solvent always flows from lower concentration (dilute) to higher concentration of solution.
questions.whyTier: It targets the most common misconception about osmosis.

questions.q: Match each term with its description.
questions.whyTier: All terms are defined in NCERT section 1.6.4.

pairs.R: Same osmotic pressure as cell fluid (0.9% NaCl)
Allows only solvent molecules to pass

questions.q: Identify the material that cannot act as a semipermeable membrane.
questions.answer: Glass sheet
questions.hint: Glass has no submicroscopic pores for solvent to pass through; the others are natural or synthetic semipermeable membranes.
questions.whyTier: It is a classification task based on NCERT examples.

questions.q: Why is osmotic pressure measurement preferred for determining the molar masses of proteins?
questions.answer: It is done at room temperature, uses molarity, and gives a large measurable value even for very dilute solutions; proteins are not stable at higher temperatures.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT 'explain why' point.

questions.q: Explain, with three everyday examples, how osmosis affects living and preserved materials.
questions.answer: 1. A raw mango placed in concentrated brine loses water by osmosis and shrivels into pickle.\n2. Wilted flowers or a limp carrot become firm again in fresh water because water enters their cells by osmosis.\n3. Salting meat or adding sugar to fruit preserves them: bacteria on them lose water by osmosis, shrivel and die.
questions.whyTier: These applications are discussed directly in NCERT.

questions.q: Starting from π = CRT, derive the expression for the molar mass M₂ of a solute from osmotic pressure data.
questions.answer:
Step 1: π = CRT, where C = n₂/V (V in litres).
Step 2: So π = (n₂/V) RT, i.e. πV = n₂ RT.
Step 3: With n₂ = w₂/M₂, πV = w₂RT/M₂, giving M₂ = w₂RT/(πV).
Condition: valid for dilute solutions; the solute must neither associate nor dissociate.
questions.whyTier: This derivation (equations 1.39–1.42) is in NCERT.

questions.q: Calculate the osmotic pressure of a 0.05 M aqueous glucose solution at 300 K. (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.answer:
Given: C = 0.05 mol L⁻¹, T = 300 K, R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Formula: π = CRT.
Substitution: π = 0.05 × 0.083 × 300.
Answer: π = 1.245 bar ≈ 1.25 bar.
questions.whyTier: It is a direct formula application with new values.

questions.q: 500 mL of an aqueous solution contains 2.0 g of a polymer. Its osmotic pressure at 27 °C is 1.0 × 10⁻³ bar. Calculate (a) the osmotic pressure in pascal and (b) the molar mass of the polymer. (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.answer:
Given: w₂ = 2.0 g, V = 500 mL = 0.500 L, π = 1.0 × 10⁻³ bar, T = 27 + 273 = 300 K.
(a) 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa, so π = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × 10⁵ Pa = 100 Pa.
(b) Formula: M₂ = w₂RT/(πV).
Substitution: M₂ = (2.0 g × 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 300 K)/(1.0 × 10⁻³ bar × 0.500 L) = 49.8/(5.0 × 10⁻⁴) g mol⁻¹.
Answer: M₂ = 9.96 × 10⁴ g mol⁻¹ (about 99,600 g mol⁻¹).
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT-style polymer molar-mass numerical (like Example 1.11) with new values.

questions.q: Sketch how the osmotic pressure of a dilute solution varies with its molarity at constant temperature. What is the slope of the graph?
questions.answer: The graph is a straight line through the origin, since π = CRT. Its slope equals RT.
questions.whyTier: It interprets the osmotic pressure formula graphically, beyond NCERT figures.

questions.q: Case Study: Choosing the right drip
questions.passage: A patient needs fluids through an intravenous drip. The nurse uses 0.9% (mass/volume) sodium chloride solution, called normal saline. A trainee asks why plain distilled water or a strong 5% salt solution cannot be used. The doctor explains using the behaviour of red blood cells in different solutions.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: What is the term for a solution like normal saline relative to blood-cell fluid?
subqs.answer: Isotonic.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: Normal saline contains 9 g NaCl per litre. What mass of NaCl is in a 250 mL drip?

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why would a 5% salt solution harm the red blood cells?
subqs.answer: It is hypertonic; water flows out of the cells by osmosis, so the cells shrink.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: What would happen if distilled water were injected? Evaluate the risk.
subqs.answer: Distilled water is hypotonic; water would enter the cells by osmosis, making them swell and possibly burst, which is dangerous.

questions.q: Reverse osmosis occurs when the pressure applied on the solution side is:
questions.hint: A pressure larger than the osmotic pressure reverses the direction of solvent flow.
questions.whyTier: It is the NCERT definition of reverse osmosis.
opts: A. Less than the osmotic pressure
B. Equal to the osmotic pressure
C. Greater than the osmotic pressure

questions.q: A workable porous membrane for reverse osmosis is a film of cellulose ________ placed over a suitable support.
questions.answer: acetate
questions.whyTier: It completes an NCERT statement.

questions.q: Cellulose acetate membranes are permeable to the ions present in sea water.
questions.answer: False
questions.hint: They are permeable to water but impermeable to impurities and ions.
questions.whyTier: It tests a detail stated in NCERT.

questions.q: Match each item with its description in reverse osmosis.
questions.whyTier: All points come from NCERT section 1.6.5.

pairs.R: Pure solvent flows out of the solution
Permeable to water, impermeable to ions

questions.q: Identify the process that does NOT use reverse osmosis.
questions.answer: Distillation of water
questions.hint: Distillation separates water by boiling and condensing, not by pressure through a membrane.
questions.whyTier: It is an application-sorting task.

questions.q: What is reverse osmosis?
questions.answer: It is the flow of pure solvent out of a solution through a semipermeable membrane when a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied to the solution side.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT definition.

questions.q: Explain how sea water is desalinated by reverse osmosis.
questions.answer: 1. Sea water is separated from pure water by a semipermeable membrane such as cellulose acetate.\n2. A pressure greater than the osmotic pressure of sea water is applied on the sea-water side.\n3. Water molecules are squeezed through the membrane to the pure-water side, while ions and impurities are held back, giving potable water.
questions.whyTier: It is a standard NCERT application (Fig. 1.11).

questions.q: Treat sea water as 0.60 M NaCl that is completely dissociated (i = 2). Estimate the minimum pressure needed for reverse osmosis at 300 K. (R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.answer:
Given: C = 0.60 mol L⁻¹, i = 2, T = 300 K, R = 0.083 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Formula: π = i C R T.
Substitution: π = 2 × 0.60 × 0.083 × 300 bar.
Answer: π ≈ 29.9 bar, so a pressure greater than about 30 bar must be applied.
questions.whyTier: It combines reverse osmosis with the van't Hoff factor, two concepts not combined in NCERT.

questions.q: Case Study: The household RO purifier
questions.passage: A family in a coastal town installs an RO water purifier because their tap water is salty. The purifier pumps water at high pressure against a thin membrane. Clean water collects in one tank while a stream of concentrated reject water drains away. The technician warns that the pump must work harder if the tap water becomes saltier.
questions.whyTier: It applies the concept to a new household scenario.

subqs.label: (a)
subqs.q: What does 'RO' stand for?
subqs.answer: Reverse osmosis.

subqs.label: (b)
subqs.q: If the osmotic pressure of the tap water is 3 bar, what is the least pressure the pump must apply?
subqs.answer: More than 3 bar.

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why is the reject water more concentrated than the tap water?
subqs.answer: Water passes through the membrane but the dissolved salts do not, so the salts stay behind in a smaller volume.

questions.q: Define the van't Hoff factor.
questions.answer: It is the ratio of normal molar mass to abnormal (experimentally determined) molar mass, or of observed to calculated colligative property.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT definition.

questions.q: Explain why ethanoic acid shows an abnormal molar mass when its freezing point depression is measured in benzene.
questions.answer: 1. In benzene, a solvent of low dielectric constant, ethanoic acid molecules dimerise through hydrogen bonding: 2CH₃COOH ⇌ (CH₃COOH)₂.\n2. Dimerisation reduces the number of solute particles, so ΔT_f (a colligative property) is smaller than expected, ideally half.\n3. Since M₂ is inversely proportional to ΔT_f, the calculated molar mass comes out higher, about twice the true value (120 instead of 60 g mol⁻¹).
questions.whyTier: It is a standard NCERT explanation.

questions.q: Derive the relation between the van't Hoff factor i and (a) the degree of dissociation α of a solute that gives n ions, and (b) the degree of association α of a solute that forms an aggregate of n molecules.
questions.answer:
(a) Dissociation:
1. Start with 1 mol of solute; α mol dissociates, each giving n particles.
2. Undissociated solute = (1 − α) mol; ions formed = nα mol.
3. Total particles = 1 − α + nα = 1 + (n − 1)α.
4. i = (particles after)/(particles before) = 1 + (n − 1)α, so α = (i − 1)/(n − 1).
(b) Association:
5. Start with 1 mol; α mol associates into aggregates of n molecules, giving α/n mol of aggregate and (1 − α) mol unassociated. Total = 1 − α + α/n, so i = 1 − α(1 − 1/n) and α = (1 − i)/(1 − 1/n).
Check: for complete dimerisation (n = 2, α = 1), i = 0.5; for KCl fully dissociated (n = 2, α = 1), i = 2.
questions.whyTier: It extends Examples 1.12–1.13 into a general derivation, a step beyond NCERT.
keyPoints: Checks: i = 2 for KCl, 0.5 for dimer

questions.q: Calculate the freezing point of a solution containing 5.85 g of NaCl in 500 g of water, assuming complete dissociation. (K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹; freezing point of water = 273.15 K)
questions.answer:
Given: w₂ = 5.85 g, M(NaCl) = 58.5 g mol⁻¹, w₁ = 0.500 kg, i = 2, K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: ΔT_f = i K_f m.
Substitution: n = 5.85/58.5 = 0.100 mol; m = 0.100/0.500 = 0.200 mol kg⁻¹; ΔT_f = 2 × 1.86 × 0.200 = 0.744 K.
Answer: T_f = 273.15 − 0.744 = 272.41 K.
questions.whyTier: It applies the modified colligative equation with new values.

questions.q: 3.0 g of benzoic acid (C₆H₅COOH, M = 122 g mol⁻¹) dissolved in 30 g of benzene lowers its freezing point by 2.36 K. K_f for benzene is 5.12 K kg mol⁻¹. Calculate (a) the experimental molar mass, (b) the van't Hoff factor and (c) the percentage association of benzoic acid if it forms dimers.
questions.answer:
Given: w₂ = 3.0 g, w₁ = 30 g, ΔT_f = 2.36 K, K_f = 5.12 K kg mol⁻¹, normal M = 122 g mol⁻¹.
(a) M₂ = (1000 × w₂ × K_f)/(ΔT_f × w₁) = (1000 × 3.0 × 5.12)/(2.36 × 30) = 15360/70.8 = 217 g mol⁻¹.
(b) i = normal molar mass / abnormal molar mass = 122/217 = 0.562.
(c) For dimerisation 2C₆H₅COOH ⇌ (C₆H₅COOH)₂: i = 1 − x/2, so x/2 = 1 − 0.562 = 0.438 and x = 0.875.
Answer: 217 g mol⁻¹; i = 0.562; degree of association = 87.5%.
questions.whyTier: It is an NCERT-style multi-step numerical modelled on Example 1.12 with new data.
keyPoints: M_obs = 1000 w₂ K_f/(ΔT_f w₁) = 217 g mol⁻¹

questions.q: A 0.10 m aqueous solution of a weak monobasic acid HA freezes at −0.205 °C. Calculate the van't Hoff factor and the degree of dissociation of the acid. (K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
questions.answer:
Given: m = 0.10 mol kg⁻¹, ΔT_f = 0.205 K, K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹.
Formula: ΔT_f = i K_f m; for HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, i = 1 + α.
Substitution: i = 0.205/(1.86 × 0.10) = 0.205/0.186 = 1.10; α = i − 1 = 0.10.
Answer: i ≈ 1.10; degree of dissociation ≈ 0.10 (10%).
questions.whyTier: It combines i with degree of dissociation, as in Example 1.13 but with new values.

questions.q: On the same axes, sketch ΔT_f against molality for aqueous solutions of urea, NaCl and K₂SO₄ (assume complete dissociation). Compare the slopes.
questions.answer: All three are straight lines through the origin, since ΔT_f = i K_f m. The slope is K_f for urea (i = 1), 2K_f for NaCl (i = 2) and 3K_f for K₂SO₄ (i = 3), so the K₂SO₄ line is steepest and the urea line least steep.
questions.whyTier: It applies the van't Hoff factor graphically, beyond NCERT.

questions.q: Case Study: When the molar mass comes out wrong
questions.passage: Two students determine molar masses by freezing point depression. One dissolves KCl (true molar mass 74.5 g mol⁻¹) in water and gets a value close to 37 g mol⁻¹. The other dissolves ethanoic acid (true molar mass 60 g mol⁻¹) in benzene and gets nearly 120 g mol⁻¹. Their teacher says neither student made an error in the experiment.
questions.whyTier: Case studies are a compulsory CBSE format.

subqs.answer: Abnormal molar masses.

subqs.label: (b)

subqs.label: (c)
subqs.q: Why did the ethanoic acid result come out about twice the true value?
subqs.answer: Ethanoic acid dimerises in benzene through hydrogen bonding, halving the number of particles and the freezing point depression, so the calculated molar mass doubles.

subqs.label: (d)
subqs.q: Would the KCl result be closer to 74.5 g mol⁻¹ in a more concentrated solution? Evaluate.
subqs.answer: Slightly, yes. Interionic attractions increase with concentration, so i falls below 2 (e.g. 1.85 at 0.1 m), making the experimental molar mass somewhat larger, but still well below 74.5 g mol⁻¹.
